CausalChain: Activated CAFs in TME -> Secretion of exosomes loaded with specific microRNAs -> Uptake of exosomal miRNAs by tumor cells -> Upregulation of IL-6 expression in tumor cells -> Enhanced activation of JAK2/STAT3 pathway -> Induction of EMT and chemoresistance -> Increased metastatic potential
Hypothesis: Exosomal microRNAs secreted by cancer-associated fibroblasts reinforce IL-6-induced JAK2/STAT3 signaling in tumor cells, establishing a feed-forward loop that promotes EMT, chemoresistance, and metastasis; thus, targeting exosomal miRNA release in combination with IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 pathway inhibitors will synergistically inhibit cancer progression.
Abstract: Recent studies have revealed that the IL‐6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling axis plays a critical role in cancer progression by promoting epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), immune evasion, and chemoresistance. In addition to direct cytokine-mediated activation, emerging evidence suggests that the tumor microenvironment, particularly cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), might contribute to the sustained activation of this pathway through alternative mechanisms. In this context, we propose a novel mechanism in which CAFs release exosomes containing specific microRNAs that, upon uptake by tumor cells, upregulate IL-6 expression and enhance JAK2/STAT3 signaling. This feed-forward loop can further drive EMT, chemoresistance, and metastasis. Therapeutically, combining strategies to inhibit both exosome-mediated microRNA transfer and the IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 axis may provide a synergistic approach to suppress tumor progression.
